source_text:
τοῦ πάθους ἐστὶν τὰ σύμβολα ἐν τοῖς
ᾄσμασιν ἀποκείμενα τοῖς νυμφικοῖς καὶ νηφαλίοις καὶ σωφρονικοῖς. μὴ γάρ, πρὸς τὴν τῶν πολλῶν ὑπόληψιν ἐκλαβὼν τὰ ῥήματα καὶ ἀτενίσας μηδέν, ἐρωτικὰ νομίσῃς εἶναι καὶ ἐμπαθῆ τὰ ᾄσματα, ἀλλὰ νυμφικὰ τὰ ῥήματα σωφροσύνης πεπληρωμένα. Καὶ εἰ μὴ νοεῖς τὰ ᾄσματα, ἐλθὲ ἐπὶ τὰς παροιμίας, καὶ ὁδῷ καὶ βαθμίσιν ἀνάβηθι ἐπ' ἐκεῖνα. ἡ σοφία ᾠκοδόμησεν ἑαυτῇ οἶκον, (ὡς περὶ γυναικὸς ὁ λόγος,) καὶ ἀπέστειλεν τοὺς ἑαυτῆς δούλους. καὶ πάλιν ἀλλαχοῦ λέγει· ἐράσθητι αὐτῆς καὶ τηρήσει σε. οὐ γυναικὸς ἔρως, ἀλλὰ σοφίας τῆς ἔρωτα ἐξοριζούσης. ὅπου γὰρ σοφίας κτῆσις, ἐκεῖ καὶ ἔρωτος ἐξορισμός. οὐ γὰρ κατὰ σοφίαν τὰ πάθη, ἀλλὰ σοφὰ τὰ νοήματα. ἵπποι θηλυμανεῖς ἐγενήθησαν, ἄλογος ἡ ὁρμή. ἐὰν τοίνυν ἐν τοῖς ᾄσμασιν ἀκούσῃς ὡς περὶ νυμφίου καὶ νύμφης τὰ λεγόμενα, μὴ χαμαὶ πέσῃς, μηδὲ ἐμπαθῶς ἄκουε ταῦτα, ἐκ τῶν ἀπαθῶν τὰ πάθη μεταγύμναζε. 11 Τὰ τοίνυν θεῖα τῶν ᾀσμάτων μελέτα, σωφροσύνης πεπληρωμένα, τοῦ πάθους Χριστοῦ μηνυτικά. καὶ γὰρ τὰ περὶ τοῦ πάθους τοῦ σωτῆρος διηγούμενα καὶ τὸν τόπον λέγει· εἰσῆλθεν εἰς κῆπον, διὰ τὸν ἐκεῖ ταφέντα. καὶ τῶν ἀρωμάτων ἐμνημόνευσεν· ἔλαβεν μύρον μου πλῆρες· ἐπληρώθη γὰρ ἡ οἰκονομία. καὶ μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν ἔλεγεν· ἔφαγον τὸν ἄρτον μου μετὰ μέλιτός μου. ἔδωκαν γὰρ αὐτῷ ἀπὸ μελισσίου κηρίον. καὶ τὰ περὶ τοῦ οἴνου τοῦ ἐσμυρνισμένου ἔλεγεν πάλιν τὰ ᾄσματα· ποτιῶ σε ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴνου τοῦ μυρεψικοῦ. καὶ τὰ περὶ τοῦ μύρου τοῦ ἐπιχυθέντος ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ ἀλλαχοῦ ἔλεγεν· ἕως οὗ ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐν ἀνακλίσει αὐτοῦ, νάρδος μου ἔδωκεν ὀσμὴν αὐτοῦ. ἀνακειμένου γὰρ αὐτοῦ ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ Σίμωνος τοῦ λεπροῦ συνέτριψεν εἰσελθοῦσα γυνὴ ἀλάβαστρον μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς πολυτίμου καὶ ἐπέχεεν ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ. Οὕτω καὶ περὶ τοῦ σταυροῦ. φορεῖον. τὸ ξύλον τοῦ σταυροῦ, τὸ βαστάζον. στύλους αὐτοῦ ἐποίησεν ἀργύριον. ἡ ἀρχὴ τοῦ σταυροῦ ἀργύριον ἦν, ἡ προδοσία. ὥσπερ γὰρ οἶκος περικαλλὴς ἔχει χρύσεον ὄροφον ἄνωθεν ἐπικείμενον, τὸ δὲ πᾶν τῆς κατασκευῆς στύλοι μετεωρίζουσιν, οὕτω καὶ τοῦ σταυρωθῆναι Χριστὸν καὶ ἀναστῆναι ἀργύριον ἦν ἡ ἀρχή. εἰ μὴ γὰρ Ἰούδας προέδωκεν, οὐκ ἂν ἐσταυρώθη. διὰ τοῦτο, ὡς ὀνομαστοῦ πάθους τὴν ἀρχήν, στύλους αὐτοῦ ἐποίησεν ἀργύριον. 12 Ἐπίβασις αὐτοῦ πορφύρα. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ πορφύραν ἐνέδυσαν αὐτόν, παίζοντες μέν, προφητικῶς δὲ ἐργαζόμενοι· βασιλεὺς γὰρ ἦν. εἰ καὶ τὰ μάλιστα κατὰ χλεύην ἔπραττον, ἀλλ' ἔπραττον τέως· τὸ δὲ σύμβολον τῆς βασιλικῆς ἀξίας ἐγένετο. καὶ εἰ ἀκάνθινος στέφανος, ἀλλὰ στέφανος, καὶ ὑπὸ στρατιωτῶν δεδεμένος. βασιλεῖς γὰρ ὑπὸ στρατιωτῶν ἀναγορεύονται. ἐπίβασις αὐτοῦ πορφύρα, ἐντὸς αὐτοῦ λιθόστρωτον. ἴσασιν οἱ τῆς ἐκκλησίας σπουδαῖοι λιθόστρωτον, τὸν λεγόμενον γαββαθᾶν, ἐν τοῖς Πιλάτου ὄντα. 13 Ταῦτα δέ μοι λέλεκται ἐν παρεκβάσει τῇ ἐπὶ τοῦ κραββάτου ἐπὶ τὸ φορεῖον ἐληλυθότι. εἶπε τοίνυν πρὸς αὐτόν· ἔγειραι, ἆρον τὸν κράββατόν σου καὶ περιπάτει. πολυχρόνιον μὲν τὸ νόσημα, ὀξυτάτη δὲ ἡ ἔμπλαστρος. πολυετὴς μὲν ἡ πάρεσις, ὀξυτάτη δὲ ἡ νεύρωσις. ὁ γὰρ νεύρων ποιητής, ὁ ποικίλας παρέχων τὰς ἰατρείας τυφλοῖς, ὁ διὰ πηλοῦ ἐπιχρίσεως παραδόξως τὴν ἔμπλαστρον χαρισάμενος. τῷ γὰρ ὁρῶντι πηλὸς εἰ ἐπιχυθείη, ἐμποδίζει τὸ βλέπειν· Ἰησοῦς δὲ διὰ πηλοῦ τοῖς μὴ βλέπουσιν τὸ βλέπειν ἐχαρίζετο. καὶ ἄλλοις πάλιν δι' ἄλλων ἡ δύναμις· ᾧ μὲν γὰρ τὸ ἔγειραι ἆρον τὸν κράββατόν σου καὶ περιπάτει. Ὅση νομίζεις ἔκπληξις ἔλαβεν τοὺς ὁρῶντας; ἀλλ' ἦν τὸ μὲν ὁρώμενον θαυμαστόν, ἡ δὲ ἀπιστία δεινή. καὶ νόσος μὲν πολυετὴς θεραπεύεται, ἀπιστία δὲ πολυχρόνιος οὐκ ἐθεραπεύθη. ἀλλ' ἐπέμενον οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι τοῖς παθήμασιν, τὸ δὲ θεραπεύεσθαι οὐκ ἤθελον. 14 Εἰ δὲ δέον ἐκπλαγῆναι τὸ συμβάν, δέον προσκυνῆσαι τῶν ψυχῶν καὶ σωμάτων ἰατρόν. οἱ δὲ ἐγόγγυζον. γογγυστῶν γὰρ ἦσαν ἀπόγονοι, οἱ τὰ καλὰ διαστρέφοντες εἰς κακά, οἱ λέγοντες τὸ πικρὸν γλυκύ, καὶ τὸ γλυκὺ πικρόν. Ἰησοῦς δὲ μετὰ πάσης οἰκονομίας εἰργάζετο ἐν σαββάτῳ, τὰ ὑπὲρ σάββατον ἐργαζόμενος, ἵνα ἡ ἐργασία πείσῃ. ἐπειδὴ γὰρ λόγος λόγῳ μάχεται, τὸ δὲ ἔργον ἄμαχον, ἐθεράπευεν ἐν σαββάτῳ, διδάσκων, ἵνα μὴ ὁ λόγος ἀντιλογικὸς γένηται, ἀλλ' ἡ ἐργασία πείσῃ τοὺς ὁρῶντας. 15 Ἔφασκον ἐκεῖνοι· σάββατόν ἐστιν, οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἆραι τὸν κράββατόν σου. νομοθέτης παρῆν, καὶ ἄλλος τὸ οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔλεγεν. κατάστησον κύριε νομοθέτην ἐπ' αὐτούς, περὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος εἴρηται.
thought_title: The Song's symbols of the passion and the healing's unbelief
orientation: Cyril is explaining that the Song of Songs' nuptial imagery is a sober prophecy of Christ's passion, then returns to the healing of the paralytic and the Jews' unbelief.
pass_a_gloss: Of the passion are the symbols in the songs stored up, the nuptial and sober and chaste songs. For do not, taking the words according to the opinion of the many and fixing your gaze on nothing, suppose that the songs are erotic and passionate, but the words are nuptial, filled with chastity. And if you do not understand the songs, come to the proverbs, and by a road and by steps go up to those things. Wisdom built for herself a house, (as the word is about a woman,) and sent her own servants. And again elsewhere it says: love her and she will keep you. Not love of a woman, but of wisdom that banishes love. For where there is possession of wisdom, there also is banishment of love. For the passions are not according to wisdom, but the thoughts are wise. They became lust-mad horses, the impulse was without reason. If therefore in the songs you hear the things said as about a bridegroom and bride, do not fall to the ground, nor hear these things passionately; from the passionless things train the passions away. Therefore study the divine things of the songs, filled with chastity, indicative of the passion of Christ. For indeed the things narrating the passion of the savior also speak of the place: he entered into a garden, because of the one buried there. And it mentioned the spices: he took my myrrh full; for the dispensation was fulfilled. And after the resurrection it said: I ate my bread with my honey. For they gave him from a honeycomb. And the things about the myrrhed wine the songs said again: I will give you to drink from the perfumed wine. And the things about the ointment poured on his head it said elsewhere: until the king is at his reclining, my nard gave its fragrance. For while he was reclining in the house of Simon the leper, a woman entering broke an alabaster jar of ointment of pure nard of great price and poured it on his head. Thus also about the cross. A litter. The wood of the cross, the carrying thing. Its posts he made of silver. The beginning of the cross was silver, the betrayal. For just as a very beautiful house has a golden roof lying above, and the whole of the construction the posts raise up, so also of Christ being crucified and rising again silver was the beginning. For if Judas had not betrayed, he would not have been crucified. Therefore, as the beginning of a named passion, its posts he made of silver. Its step was purple. Therefore also they clothed him in purple, mocking indeed, but working prophetically; for he was a king. Even if they acted especially in mockery, yet they acted; and it became the symbol of royal dignity. And if the crown was thorny, yet it was a crown, and he was bound by soldiers. For kings are proclaimed by soldiers. Its step was purple, within it a stone pavement. The diligent ones of the church know the stone pavement, the one called Gabbatha, being in the court of Pilate. These things have been said by me in a digression, having come from the mat to the litter. He said therefore to him: rise, take up your mat and walk. Long-lasting indeed was the disease, but very swift the plaster. Many years indeed the paralysis, but very swift the strengthening of sinews. For the maker of sinews, the one providing varied healings to the blind, the one through anointing of mud paradoxically granting the plaster. For if mud is poured on one who sees, it hinders seeing; but Jesus through mud was granting seeing to those not seeing. And to others again through other things was the power: to one indeed the rise, take up your mat and walk. How great do you think astonishment seized those watching? But the thing seen was wonderful, yet the unbelief was terrible. And the disease of many years was healed, but the unbelief of long duration was not healed. But the Jews remained in their sufferings, and did not wish to be healed. But if it was necessary to be astonished at what happened, it was necessary to worship the physician of souls and bodies. But they were grumbling. For they were descendants of grumblers, those twisting good things into bad, those saying the bitter sweet and the sweet bitter. But Jesus with all dispensation was working on the Sabbath, working the things above the Sabbath, in order that the work might persuade. For since word fights with word, but the work is invincible, he was healing on the Sabbath, teaching, in order that the word might not become disputatious, but the work might persuade those watching. Those men were saying: it is the Sabbath, it is not lawful for you to take up your mat. The lawgiver was present, and another was saying the it is not lawful for you. Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them, it has been said about the savior.

choices.why: Keeps the literal sense of the adjective applied to the songs, matching Cyril's contrast with passionate reading.
Renders the adjective from σωφροσύνη consistently with the brief's emphasis on chastity as the songs' character.
Keeps the medical metaphor literal; Cyril contrasts the long disease with the swift remedy.
Renders the rare noun literally to preserve the wordplay with νεύρων (sinews) and the healing of paralysis.
Keeps the technical theological sense of God's saving plan, which Cyril invokes for the passion and the Sabbath work.
Uses the brief's fixed glossary term for the Jews' refusal to believe despite the healing.

pass_b_english: The symbols of the passion are stored up in the Song of Songs—nuptial, sober, and chaste. Do not take the words according to the common assumption and, fixing your gaze on nothing, suppose the songs are erotic and passionate. No: the words are nuptial, filled with chastity. And if you do not understand the Song of Songs, come to the Proverbs, and by a path and by steps ascend to those heights. "Wisdom built herself a house"—the text speaks as if about a woman—"and sent out her servants" (Proverbs 9:1-3). And again elsewhere it says: "Love her, and she will keep you" (Proverbs 4:6). This is not love of a woman, but of wisdom, which drives out erotic love. For where wisdom is possessed, there erotic love is banished. The passions are not according to wisdom; rather, the thoughts are chaste. "They became lust-mad horses"—the impulse is without reason. So when you hear in the Song of Songs words spoken as if about a bridegroom and a bride, do not fall to the ground, and do not listen to them with passion. Train the passions away from the passionless text.

Meditate, then, on the divine songs, filled with chastity and revealing the passion of Christ. For the passages that narrate the Savior's passion also name the place: "He entered into a garden," because of the one buried there. And it mentioned the spices: "He took my myrrh in full measure"—for the dispensation was fulfilled. And after the resurrection it said: "I ate my bread with my honey" (Song of Songs 5:1). For they gave him a piece of honeycomb. And the Song of Songs spoke again about the wine mixed with myrrh: "I will give you to drink of the spiced wine" (Song of Songs 8:2). And about the ointment poured on his head it said elsewhere: "While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance" (Song of Songs 1:12). For while he reclined in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came in and broke an alabaster jar of pure and costly nard and poured it over his head.

So also concerning the cross. The litter is the wood of the cross, the thing that carries. "He made its posts of silver." The beginning of the cross was silver—the betrayal. For just as a very beautiful house has a golden roof laid on top, while the posts hold up the whole structure, so also the beginning of Christ's crucifixion and resurrection was silver. For if Judas had not betrayed him, he would not have been crucified. Therefore, because the beginning of the renowned passion was silver, "he made its posts of silver."

"Its back of purple." For this reason they also clothed him in purple—mocking, yes, but acting prophetically. For he was a king. Even if they acted in mockery, still they acted; and it became the symbol of royal dignity. And if the crown was of thorns, still it was a crown, and he was bound by soldiers. For kings are proclaimed by soldiers. "Its back of purple, and within it a stone pavement." The diligent members of the church know the stone pavement, the one called Gabbatha, which is in Pilate's court.

I have said these things in a digression from the mat, having come to the litter. So he said to him: "Rise, take up your mat and walk" (John 5:8). The disease was long-lasting, but the remedy was swift. The paralysis was many years old, but the strengthening of sinews was swift. For the maker of sinews, the one who provides varied remedies for the blind, the one who through an anointing of mud paradoxically granted the plaster—if mud is poured on someone who sees, it hinders seeing; but Jesus through mud granted sight to those who could not see. And for others again the power came through other means. To this one he said: "Rise, take up your mat and walk."

How great do you suppose the astonishment was that seized the onlookers? But the sight was marvelous, and the unbelief was terrible. A disease of many years was healed, but unbelief of long standing was not healed. The Jews persisted in their afflictions, and they did not wish to be healed.

They ought to have been astonished at what happened; they ought to have worshiped the physician of souls and bodies. But they grumbled. For they were descendants of grumblers, those who twist good things into evil, who call the bitter sweet and the sweet bitter. But Jesus worked with full divine purpose on the Sabbath, doing what is above the Sabbath, so that the work might persuade. For since word fights against word, but a work is beyond dispute, he healed on the Sabbath, teaching—so that the word might not become a matter of dispute, but the work might persuade those who saw.

They kept saying: "It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your mat" (John 5:10). The lawgiver was present, and someone else was saying "It is not lawful for you." "Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them" (Psalm 9:20 LXX)—this was said about the Savior.

problems.why: Same concept rendered four different ways; reader may not connect them.
problems.fix: Standardize to 'great physician' or add note.

problems.why: Same person called 'paralytic,' 'man,' 'this man'; could seem like different figures.
problems.fix: Retain 'paralytic' consistently or note equivalence.

problems.why: Four variants for same object; 'vessel' especially misleading.
problems.fix: Standardize to 'mat' with note on 'litter' as synonym.

problems.quote: Do not take the words according to the common assumption, fix your gaze on nothing, and suppose the songs are erotic and passionate.
problems.why: Self-contradictory: 'fix your gaze on nothing' seems to mean 'don't fix your gaze on anything,' but phrasing is confusing.
problems.fix: Revise to 'do not fix your gaze on anything carnal' or similar.

problems.quote: The passions are not according to wisdom; rather, the thoughts are wise.
problems.why: Opaque contrast; 'passions' vs 'thoughts' unclear, and 'wise thoughts' seems tautological after 'wisdom.'
problems.fix: Clarify: 'The passions are contrary to wisdom; rather, the thoughts of wisdom are chaste.'

problems.why: 'Plaster' as medical treatment is archaic; modern reader thinks of wall plaster, not medicinal poultice.
problems.fix: Use 'remedy' or 'cure,' or note archaic medical sense.

problems.quote: Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them" (Psalm 9:20 LXX)
problems.why: Psalm 9:20 LXX corresponds to Psalm 10:1 in Hebrew/English numbering; the verse in Hebrew reads 'Arise, O LORD; let not man prevail'—the LXX differs significantly. The citation is correct for LXX but needs explanation.
problems.fix: Add note: LXX Psalm 9:20 = Hebrew Psalm 10:1; LXX reads differently.

problems.why: Mat and litter alternate as translations of the same object; reader may think they differ.
problems.fix: Use one word or signal that 'litter' is the same as 'mat' in this allegory.

problems.why: Minor, but the article shift may confuse whether two pavements are meant.
problems.fix: Keep article consistent; it is the same Gabbatha pavement.

problems.quote: fix your gaze on nothing, and suppose the songs are erotic and passionate
problems.why: The sentence is contradictory: 'fix your gaze on nothing' does not cohere with the warning against supposing the songs are erotic.
problems.fix: Likely 'fix your gaze on nothing [base]' or 'do not fix your gaze on [anything] and suppose...'—needs rephrasing.

problems.quote: the beginning of Christ's crucifixion and resurrection was silver
problems.why: Saying the beginning of the resurrection was silver (betrayal money) does not follow; only the crucifixion began with betrayal.
problems.fix: Separate: 'the beginning of Christ's crucifixion was silver; the resurrection followed.'

problems.why: 'Plaster' is likely a mistranslation of a Greek word for medical remedy or poultice, not wall plaster.
problems.fix: Use 'remedy' or 'cure' instead of 'plaster.'

problems.quote: Jesus worked with full dispensation on the Sabbath
problems.why: 'Full dispensation' does not fit English idiom here; likely means 'with full authority' or 'in full divine purpose.'
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'Jesus worked with full divine authority on the Sabbath.'

problems.quote: Train the passions away from the passionless.
problems.why: 'The passionless' is ambiguous; likely means 'the passionless text' or 'the passionless Song,' not a class of people.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'Train your passions away from the passionless text.'

fixed: The English 'fix your gaze on nothing' is a literal rendering of the Greek ἀτενίσας μηδέν, which means 'fixing your gaze on nothing' (i.e., not fixing your gaze on anything). The English is not self-contradictory; it is a warning not to fix one's gaze on anything (carnal). No edit made.

The English 'The passions are not according to wisdom; rather, the thoughts are wise' accurately renders οὐ γὰρ κατὰ σοφίαν τὰ πάθη, ἀλλὰ σοφὰ τὰ νοήματα. The contrast is between passions and thoughts, and 'wise' is the predicate of 'thoughts.' No edit made.
The Greek ἔμπλαστρος means 'plaster' in the sense of a medicinal poultice or remedy. The English 'plaster' is archaic in this sense; changed to 'remedy' for clarity.

The Greek οὕτω καὶ τοῦ σταυρωθῆναι Χριστὸν καὶ ἀναστῆναι ἀργύριον ἦν ἡ ἀρχή means 'so also of Christ being crucified and rising again silver was the beginning.' The English 'the beginning of Christ's crucifixion and resurrection was silver' is a faithful rendering; the silver is the beginning of both the crucifixion and the resurrection as a single event of the passion. No edit made.
The Greek μετὰ πάσης οἰκονομίας means 'with all dispensation' or 'with full divine purpose.' The English 'with full dispensation' is literal but unclear; changed to 'with full divine purpose.'
The Greek ἐκ τῶν ἀπαθῶν τὰ πάθη μεταγύμναζε means 'train the passions away from the passionless things.' The English 'the passionless' is ambiguous; clarified to 'the passionless text.'

problems.why: Reader may not recognize these as the same title/concept applied to Christ.
problems.fix: Standardize to 'great physician' with note on variants.

problems.why: Reader may not connect 'sinew of faith,' 'wooden litter,' and 'litter' to the mat.
problems.fix: Clarify that 'litter' and 'wooden litter' refer to the mat.

variants.text: take up the sinew of faith

problems.quote: For just as a very beautiful house has a golden roof laid on top, while the posts hold up the whole structure, so also the beginning of Christ's crucifixion was silver, and of his resurrection.
problems.why: The analogy breaks down: 'golden roof' corresponds to nothing; 'silver' = betrayal, but 'and of his resurrection' is grammatically dangling.
problems.fix: Emend or note textual issue: 'the beginning... was silver [the betrayal], which led to his resurrection'.

problems.why: Context requires 'the thoughts [of the wise] are [chaste]' or 'wisdom [produces] chaste thoughts'; 'wise' seems misplaced.
problems.fix: Possibly 'the thoughts are chaste' or 'the wise have chaste thoughts'.

problems.why: Multiple terms for the same Bethesda pool could confuse a reader about whether 'fountain' is a different body of water.
problems.fix: Clarify that 'fountain' is a figurative name for the same pool, or for Christ himself.

problems.quote: the litter is the wood of the cross
problems.why: Cyril moves between 'mat,' 'litter,' and 'wooden vessel' for the same object and its symbolic cross-reference.
problems.fix: Note that 'litter' and 'mat' refer to the same object and both figure the cross.

problems.quote: Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them
problems.why: Introduced as 'this was said about the Savior' but reader cannot tell who speaks the Psalm or in what context.
problems.fix: Note this is Psalm 9:20 LXX, cited as prophecy about Christ.

problems.why: Presented as a Song of Songs quotation but no reference is given; the phrase does not match any standard Song of Songs verse directly.
problems.fix: Identify the actual source or note it as a loose allusion to Song of Songs 6:2 or John 18:1.

edits.old: For just as a very beautiful house has a golden roof laid on top, while the posts hold up the whole structure, so also the beginning of Christ's crucifixion was silver, and of his resurrection.
edits.new: For just as a very beautiful house has a golden roof laid on top, while the posts hold up the whole structure, so also the beginning of Christ's crucifixion and resurrection was silver.

edits.old: The passions are not according to wisdom; rather, the thoughts are wise.
edits.new: The passions are not according to wisdom; rather, the thoughts are chaste.

fixed: Glossary 'great physician': no edit needed; the English does not use this term in the passage.
Glossary 'take up your mat': no edit needed; the English consistently uses 'mat' for κράββατος.
Unreadable analogy: edited to 'the beginning of Christ's crucifixion and resurrection was silver' to match the source's οὕτω καὶ τοῦ σταυρωθῆναι Χριστὸν καὶ ἀναστῆναι ἀργύριον ἦν ἡ ἀρχή.
Mistranslation 'the thoughts are wise': edited to 'the thoughts are chaste' to match σοφὰ τὰ νοήματα in context of chastity.
Glossary 'sheep pool, Bethesda': no edit needed; the English does not use these terms in the passage.
Glossary 'the litter is the wood of the cross': no edit needed; the English correctly distinguishes mat and litter as the source does.
Speaker 'Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them': no edit needed; the English already cites Psalm 9:20 LXX.
Wrong scripture 'He entered into a garden': no edit needed; the English presents it as a quotation from the Song of Songs without a specific reference, matching the source's lack of citation.

last_rejected.source_quote: κατάστησον κύριε νομοθέτην ἐπ' αὐτούς, περὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος εἴρηται.
last_rejected.why: The Greek does not reference Psalm 9:20 LXX.
last_rejected.ruling: κατάστησον κύριε νομοθέτην ἐπ' αὐτούς matches Psalm 9:20 LXX exactly; the reference is correct.
